title: Economic equilibrium

definition.text: A state in which the forces of supply and demand balance, so that prices and quantities stop changing.

facts.text: In a market equilibrium, competition sets a price at which the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers produce.
That price is called the competitive or market-clearing price, and it tends to stay put unless demand or supply changes.
The idea was borrowed from the physical sciences, where balanced forces mean that nothing further changes.
Huw Dixon proposed three properties: agents' behaviour is consistent, no agent wants to change its behaviour, and the equilibrium results from a stable dynamic process.
A price above equilibrium creates a glut that pushes prices down; a price below it creates a shortage that pushes prices up.
When the conditions of demand or supply change, the curves shift and the equilibrium price and quantity change too.
Economists such as Paul Samuelson warn that an equilibrium price is not automatically good: a food market can be in equilibrium while people starve.
During Ireland's Great Famine of 1845–52, food was exported while people starved because the market price was above what Irish farmers could afford.

contested_note: The classical view that free markets always clear on their own has been challenged by economists who point to lasting unemployment and credit rationing.

definition.text: The condition of a market that is not in equilibrium, where the amounts supplied and demanded are out of balance.

facts.text: Disequilibrium can last only a moment or persist for a long time.
Many economists see labour markets as stuck in excess supply over long periods.
Some goods' prices adjust slowly because of menu costs and long-term contracts, but they do not stay out of balance forever.

definition.text: An equilibrium in which several quantities keep growing at the same rate, so that the ratios between them stay fixed.

facts.text: In the neoclassical growth model, output and capital grow at the same rate as the workforce, leaving output per worker unchanged.
Comparing two dynamic equilibria is called comparative dynamics.
In that model a permanently higher saving rate raises capital per worker but leaves the growth rate of output unchanged.

definition.text: The total gain that buyers and sellers get from trading in a market, made up of consumer surplus and producer surplus; also called total or social welfare.

facts.text: The sum of consumer and producer surplus is called social or total surplus, and a fall in that total caused by inefficiency is called deadweight loss.
The engineer Jules Dupuit first put forward the idea in the mid-19th century, and the economist Alfred Marshall made it famous.
It is also called Marshallian surplus, after Alfred Marshall.
On a supply and demand diagram, consumer surplus is the area above the price and below the demand curve, and producer surplus the area below the price and above the supply curve.
Early writers used surplus to study food: farming must feed everyone, so the rest of the economy is limited by the food farmers produce beyond their own needs.

definition.text: The gap between the most a buyer would be willing to pay for something and the price they actually pay.

facts.text: Drinking water usually carries a large consumer surplus: people would pay very high prices for it because they need it to survive.
The first few liters of water are worth the most, since they prevent death, so they hold more surplus than later liters.
Buyers value each extra unit less than the last, yet pay the same market price for every unit, which is where the surplus comes from.
It equals the area under the demand curve and above the price; with a straight-line demand curve it is a triangle, otherwise it is found by integration.
A positive change in consumer surplus after a price change is read as a gain in the person's welfare, a negative change as a loss.
When supply grows and the price falls, existing buyers gain on the units they already bought and new buyers enter and gain too.

definition.text: The gain sellers get when the market price is higher than the least they would accept to supply a good.

facts.text: It is roughly equal to profit, since producers will not normally sell at a loss.
It is shown as the area below the market price line and above the supply curve.
Higher market prices raise it; higher production costs or lower prices shrink it, and taxes, subsidies, new technology and competition can shift it.
It is used to judge how taxes, subsidies, price controls and trade policies affect producers.

definition.text: A shortcut that estimates the change in consumer surplus from a small change in supply when the demand curve stays the same.

facts.text: With straight-line demand, the change in surplus is a trapezoid whose height is the price change and whose middle width is the average of the quantities before and after.

definition.text: Any arrangement that lets buyers and sellers exchange goods, services and information.

facts.text: An exchange of goods or services, with or without money, is called a transaction.
Markets let tradeable things be valued and priced, which is how they spread resources around a society.
Economists see a market as a coordinating mechanism that uses prices to pass information among firms, households and individuals; using prices this way is its defining feature.
A market can arise more or less on its own or be built on purpose, and most rely on sellers swapping goods or labour for buyers' money rather than barter.
Markets range from one building's food market to a city's housing market, a whole country, or worldwide trades such as diamonds.
Some markets are created by regulation to tackle side effects such as pollution, for example markets in pollution permits.
When a market's equilibrium is not efficient, economists say a market failure has occurred, though government fixes can fail too.
Prices can be distorted by a seller with monopoly power or a buyer with monopsony power, which lowers welfare and efficiency.

title: Market size

definition.text: How big a market is, measured either by its number of buyers and sellers or by the money exchanged in it, usually per year.

facts.text: Measured in money, market size is often called market value.
The same goods can have different, usually rising, market values at the production, wholesale and retail levels.

notes: Thin; candidate for trimming at selection.

title: Willingness to pay

definition.text: The highest price at which a person will definitely buy one unit of something.

facts.text: It matches the standard economic idea of a consumer's reservation price, though some researchers treat it as a range.
It depends on context: people will pay more for a soft drink at a luxury resort than at a beach bar or a local shop.
Jules Dupuit argued that adding up each user's willingness to pay measures the social benefit of a bridge, road or canal.
Cost–benefit analysis turns hard-to-price impacts into money using willingness to pay, though these are often hard to estimate.
Stated-preference methods such as contingent valuation ask people directly what they would pay for an ecosystem or one of its services.
The value of a statistical life tries to estimate how much people would pay to lower their risk of dying, and is used to cost deaths from air pollution.
People's maximum willingness to pay for an object is typically lower than the least they would accept to give it up once they own it.

notes: Own page is thin (6 sentences); facts drawn mostly from other pages.

definition.text: The loss of society's welfare when a good is produced or consumed at a quantity where its benefit to society does not equal its cost to society.

facts.text: It is the net benefit nobody gets: either goods are made that cost more than they are worth, or worthwhile goods are not made.
Unlike most losses, which are someone else's gain, deadweight loss is regained by no one.
It can come from monopoly pricing, externalities, taxes or subsidies, or binding price ceilings and floors such as a minimum wage.
If nails cost $0.10 to make and a monopolist charges $0.60, buyers who value a nail between those prices are shut out, and their lost benefit is the deadweight loss.
A $0.03 subsidy on that nail lowers its price to $0.07, so people who value it below its true $0.10 cost buy it, which also wastes resources.
In a cleaning deal worth $40 of total surplus, a $50 tax stops the trade entirely; the lost $40 is the deadweight loss, and the government collects nothing.
The more elastic supply and demand are, the bigger the deadweight loss from a tax.
Deadweight loss grows with the square of a tax: doubling the tax multiplies the loss by 4.

title: Harberger's triangle

definition.text: The triangle on a supply and demand graph that shows the deadweight loss from government intervention in an otherwise perfect market.

facts.text: It is generally credited to Arnold Harberger, and the interventions include price floors, caps, taxes, tariffs and quotas.
It also measures the loss from a government's failure to step into a market with externalities.
A tax drives a wedge between what buyers pay and sellers receive, and the triangle's area is the surplus lost for good.
Martin Feldstein holds these losses can drag down long-run growth, while James Tobin argued their effect on the economy is small.

contested_note: Economists disagree on whether these triangles seriously harm long-run growth (Feldstein) or matter little (Tobin).

title: Marginal cost

definition.text: The extra total cost of producing one more unit of output.

facts.text: It differs from average cost, which is total cost divided by the number of units made.
It counts only costs that change with output: for one more car, the labour and parts, but not the factory building.
Because fixed costs do not change with output, doubling them leaves marginal cost, and the profit-maximizing price and quantity, unchanged.
In the short run it eventually rises, as more labour and materials press against a fixed building and machinery.
A competitive firm keeps producing as long as the sale price exceeds the marginal cost, stopping where the two are equal.
The marginal cost curve crosses the average total cost and average variable cost curves at their lowest points.
With economies of scale, pricing at marginal cost fails to cover total costs and so needs a subsidy.
In a survey of 200 executives, 11% said their marginal costs rose with output, 48% said they were constant and 41% said they fell.

contested_note: Textbook models assume marginal cost rises with output, but many empirical studies find it constant or falling for most firms.

definition.text: A market in which a single person or company is the only supplier of a particular good or service.

facts.text: A monopoly lacks competition and close substitutes, so it can charge a price well above its marginal cost and earn high profits.
Size is not what defines it: a small business can still raise prices in a small market.
Monopolies get their power from barriers to entry, which may be economic, legal or deliberate.
A monopolist picks the output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, aiming at the largest total profit rather than the highest price.
Compared with perfect competition it sells less at a higher price, and the trades it forgoes create a deadweight loss.
Contestable-market theory says a monopoly may act as if it faced competition when entry barriers are low.
Governments respond by taking monopoly profits, breaking up the firm or changing rules to curb anti-competitive behaviour.
The word first appears in Aristotle's Politics, describing Thales of Miletus cornering the market in olive presses.

title: Natural monopoly

definition.text: A firm whose average cost of production keeps falling across the whole range of market demand, so one large supplier is cheaper than several small ones.

facts.text: Such markets, left alone, tend to turn into a monopoly, often after an early entrant expands fast and drives out rivals.
J.S. Mill first called monopolies 'natural' in 1848, citing gas and water supply, roads, canals and railways.
Breaking them up is inefficient by definition, so governments mostly use regulation and public ownership.
Regulators often impose average-cost pricing, which removes excess profit but weakens the incentive to cut costs.

notes: A page 'Natural monopoly' is also crawled; the merge may prefer it.

definition.text: A monopoly created when a government gives one person or company the exclusive right to supply something.

facts.text: It can be granted by a law that excludes rivals, or indirectly through patents, trademarks and copyright.
States grant them to reward risky investment or to enrich a domestic interest group.
A publisher can use its copyright monopoly to charge American students more than Ethiopian students for the same textbook.

definition.text: The rule that a monopoly's markup, as a share of its price, is inversely proportional to the price elasticity of demand it faces.

facts.text: The markup is measured by the Lerner index: price minus marginal cost, divided by price, equals minus one over the elasticity of demand.
Perfectly competitive firms have zero market power and simply take the market price.

title: Perfect competition

definition.text: An idealized market with many buyers and sellers, identical products and full information, so that no one can influence the price.

facts.text: Under its conditions a market reaches an equilibrium where supply equals demand for every product, including labour, and this equilibrium is Pareto optimal.
Every profit-maximizing firm ends up charging a price equal to its marginal cost, which makes the market allocatively efficient.
Without externalities and public goods, such equilibria are Pareto-efficient: a result called the First Theorem of Welfare Economics.
Each firm faces a perfectly elastic demand curve, so it must take the market price.
In the long run no firm earns economic profit, because any profit draws in new firms until the price falls to average cost.
Real markets come close to it mainly for farm products and raw materials sold by many sellers to many buyers.
Critics say it treats firms as passive, ignoring price-cutting, product design, advertising and innovation, and leaves unclear who actually sets prices.

contested_note: Critics dispute the realism of its assumptions and whether a model of price-takers can describe a decentralized market at all.

definition.text: The return that just makes running a business worthwhile, equal to what the owner's time and capital could earn in their next best use.

facts.text: Economists count normal profit as a cost, not as part of business profit.
It varies within and across industries in line with how risky each kind of investment is.
Under perfect competition only normal profits survive in the long run, so firms have no reason to enter or leave the industry.
Profits above normal persist only where barriers to entry stop new firms from coming in, as in monopoly or oligopoly.

definition.text: The price below which a loss-making firm does better to stop producing in the short run: the point where price falls under average variable cost.

facts.text: Shutting down avoids variable costs but not fixed costs, which must be paid anyway and so are ignored in the decision.
A competitive firm's short-run supply curve is its marginal cost curve at and above the shutdown point.

definition.text: The amount of money buyers are willing and able to pay for a good or service and that sellers are willing to accept.

facts.text: Prices are shaped by production costs, by supply and by demand, and may be set by a monopolist or imposed by market conditions.
Price theory says that in a free market the price settles where the quantity supplied equals the quantity demanded.
Milton Friedman named five functions of prices, including passing on information, giving incentives to produce what is valued, and rationing fixed supplies among consumers.
Price is what the buyer pays; cost of production is the seller's own spending on making the product, and the two are different things.
Adam Smith's diamond–water paradox asks why diamonds cost more than water, though water is essential to life and diamonds are mere ornament.
Carl Menger's theory of marginal utility was offered as one answer to that paradox.
In April 2020 the price of West Texas Intermediate crude for May delivery turned negative for the first time, at -$37.63 a barrel.

definition.text: A price below zero, where the owner or producer pays the 'buyer' to take an item away.

facts.text: In April 2020 oil for May delivery fell to -$37.63 a barrel, a one-day drop of $55.90, because holders feared there was nowhere left to store it.
Negative interest rates are a similar idea.

definition.text: A measure of how strongly the quantity people buy responds to a change in its price: the percentage change in quantity for a one percent change in price.

facts.text: An elasticity of −2 means a one percent price rise cuts the quantity demanded by two percent.
If quantity falls 20 tons from 200 tons after the price rises $5 from $100, quantity drops 10% and price rises 5%, giving an elasticity of −2.
Demand is inelastic when the elasticity is below one in absolute value and elastic when it is above one.
Demand is more elastic when close substitutes exist, and less elastic for necessities such as insulin or for broad categories such as food in general.
Elasticity grows with time: after a lasting fuel price rise, more people switch to carpooling or public transport.
For inelastic goods a price rise increases revenue; for elastic goods it lowers revenue, and revenue peaks where elasticity is exactly one.
Elasticity predicts who bears a tax: with perfectly inelastic demand consumers pay all of it, with perfectly elastic demand firms pay all of it.
Alfred Marshall is credited with defining elasticity of demand in his Principles of Economics of 1890.

definition.text: An elasticity measured between two points on a demand curve, using the average of the two prices and the two quantities as the base.

facts.text: It removes the problem that an ordinary elasticity depends on which point is treated as the starting one, and gives an average elasticity over that arc of the curve.
Hugh Dalton introduced it very early on.
Point elasticity instead uses calculus to measure elasticity for a tiny price change at a single point, but needs the demand formula to be known.

title: Supply and demand

definition.text: The basic economic model of how a market sets prices: the price moves until the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer.

facts.text: The idea of supply and demand is the theoretical foundation of modern economics.
The equilibrium is the price and quantity where the demand and supply curves cross.
Under perfect competition supply follows marginal cost: firms produce more as long as the extra cost is below the market price.
Consumers buy another unit as long as its value to them is more than its price, so the demand curve slopes downward.
Augustin Cournot first drew demand curves in 1838, Fleeming Jenkin added supply curves in 1870, and Alfred Marshall popularized both in 1890.
The fourteenth-century scholar Ibn Taymiyyah wrote that when desire for goods rises while availability falls, the price rises.
The model also explains wages: workers supply labour, businesses demand it, and the equilibrium price is the wage rate.
Where a seller or buyer has market power, models such as oligopoly or monopsony fit better.

contested_note: Sraffa questioned the consistency of partial-equilibrium supply curves, and Post-Keynesians argue the model fails to explain prices that firms set by mark-up.

title: Shifts in supply and demand
article: Supply and demand#Changes in market equilibrium

definition.text: Changes in conditions other than a good's own price that move a whole supply or demand curve, and so change the equilibrium price and quantity.

facts.text: A movement along a curve is a 'change in quantity demanded', while a shift of the whole curve is a 'change in demand'.
Demand can rise because of changing tastes, higher incomes, price changes in substitutes and complements, expectations or more buyers; a rise lifts both equilibrium price and quantity.
A cheaper way of growing wheat shifts supply outward, lowering the price and raising the quantity sold.
A rise in raw-material costs shifts supply to the left, so less is offered at every price.

definition.text: Comparing two economic outcomes, one before and one after a change in some outside factor, once the economy has settled into its new equilibrium.

facts.text: It compares the two equilibria but does not study the path or process of change between them.
It is used to study shifts in supply and demand in one market, and changes in monetary or fiscal policy for a whole economy.
John R. Hicks (1939) and Paul A. Samuelson (1947) formalized it, though it had been drawn in graphs since at least the 1870s.
Results usually come from a linear approximation of the equilibrium equations, which assumes the equilibrium is stable.
Because of that approximation, its results hold only for very small changes in the outside variables.
For models of steady growth, the counterpart is comparative dynamics.
The envelope theorem describes how the value of an optimal solution changes with a parameter.
Claude Berge's 1963 maximum theorem describes when the optimal solution varies continuously with the parameters.

title: Competition

definition.text: Rivalry among firms for customers and limited resources, using price, product, promotion and place.

facts.text: Classical economists held that competition pushes firms to develop new products and technologies, giving consumers more choice and better goods.
More choice usually means lower prices than under monopoly or oligopoly.
How much competition exists depends on the number of firms, barriers to entry, information, and access to resources.
Competition arises from scarcity: there is never enough to satisfy every human want.
In 1776 Adam Smith described it as steering productive resources to their most valued uses and encouraging efficiency.
Share and foreign-exchange markets are usually seen as close to perfect, while real estate is a very imperfect market.
Competition duplicates fixed costs, so for a few goods having many firms is itself inefficient: these are natural monopolies.

contested_note: Economists debate how relevant perfect competition is to real markets and whether it should serve as the benchmark.

title: Oligopoly

definition.text: A market in which a few sellers control pricing.

facts.text: Each firm's actions affect the others and provoke reactions, so the firms are mutually interdependent.
Oligopolists often collude to maximize profits, by price-fixing or by forming cartels that keep new firms out.
Competition laws mostly catch formal collusion such as cartels, so firms can escape through tacit collusion.
A duopoly is an oligopoly of only two firms.
Industries cited as oligopolistic include civil aviation, electricity supply, telecommunications, sugar refining, beer making, and pulp and paper.

notes: Page crawled but not seeded in any dossier; drafted from its lead and the Competition (economics) section.

definition.text: An equilibrium of a market with flexible prices and many traders, each too small to move prices, in which every trader gets the best bundle they can afford and supply equals demand; also called Walrasian equilibrium.

facts.text: Kenneth Arrow and Gérard Debreu introduced the concept in 1951, and it serves as economics' benchmark of efficiency.
If Alice values her car at 10 and Bob at 20, any price between 10 and 20 is an equilibrium price at which Bob buys the car.
The Arrow–Debreu model shows such an equilibrium exists in any exchange economy with divisible goods when everyone's preferences are strictly convex.
By the welfare theorems, every competitive equilibrium allocation is Pareto efficient, and every efficient allocation can be reached by one.
At this equilibrium the value society puts on a good equals the value of resources used to make it: marginal benefit equals marginal cost.
Efficiency here says nothing about fairness: an allocation where one person has everything can still be efficient.

definition.text: An ascending auction that finds a competitive equilibrium by raising the price of any item more than one buyer wants until each item is wanted by at most one buyer.

facts.text: The auctioneer starts all prices at zero and buyers name their favourite bundle at each round of prices.
Such mechanisms are also called Walrasian tâtonnement or English auctions.

title: Cost curve

definition.text: A graph showing a firm's production costs against the total quantity it produces.

facts.text: Profit-maximizing firms use cost curves to decide how much to produce.
There are total, average, marginal, fixed and variable cost curves, some for the short run and some for the long run.
Fixed cost is a flat line, while average fixed cost falls as output grows because the same cost is spread over more units.
Short-run marginal cost first falls and then rises because of diminishing marginal returns; the long-run curve is shaped by returns to scale.
When marginal cost is below average cost, average cost falls; when above, it rises; where they are equal, average cost is lowest.
In a 1952 survey of 334 companies, 95% of managers reported constant or falling costs rather than the textbook U-shape.

contested_note: Textbooks draw U-shaped cost curves, but surveys of firms suggest most face constant or falling costs.

definition.text: A measure of how the quantity demanded of one good responds to a change in the price of another good.

facts.text: A positive value means the goods are substitutes; a negative value means they are complements; zero means they are unrelated.
The cross elasticity of butter with respect to margarine is 0.81: a 1% rise in margarine's price raises butter demand by 0.81%.
Fuel and new cars are complements, so a rise in fuel prices lowers demand for cars.
Governments use cross elasticities between drinks when setting alcohol taxes and minimum prices to reduce harmful drinking.

definition.text: The quantity of a good that people are willing and able to buy at various prices over a given period.

facts.text: Demand is not the same as desire: it means both wanting something and being able to pay for it.
It is a flow, measured per unit of time, not a single purchase.
The most important influence is the good's own price: normally, the lower the price, the more people buy.
Demand also depends on the prices of complements and substitutes, income, tastes, expectations, population size, climate and government policy.
If consumers expect a price rise, they buy more now to avoid paying more later.
Goods with no substitutes, such as insulin, have nearly perfectly inelastic demand: price barely changes how much is bought.
E. F. Schumacher challenged the assumption that meeting demand is the purpose of economic activity, distinguishing wise demands for genuine needs from unwise ones.

definition.text: The demand facing one particular firm: the market demand left unmet by other firms at each price.

facts.text: It equals market demand minus the supply of the other firms at each price.
With many firms, each firm's demand is extremely elastic and nearly flat, though not perfectly flat as textbooks draw it.

definition.text: A graph showing how much of a good people will buy at each price, with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis.

facts.text: It can show one consumer's demand or, added up across everyone, the whole market's demand.
It normally slopes down because of the law of demand; exceptions include Veblen goods, Giffen goods and speculative bubbles.
A price change moves buyers along the curve; a change in anything else, such as income, related goods' prices, population or expectations, shifts the whole curve.
When incomes rise, demand for normal goods shifts out while demand for inferior goods shifts in.
If hamburgers get dearer, demand for chicken (a substitute) shifts out and demand for ketchup (a complement) shifts in.
Demand curves are estimated statistically from past data, but only one point on the curve can be observed at any one time.

definition.text: Demand for an input that comes from demand for the final product it helps make.

facts.text: An intermediate good is one used to make another, final good.
The link is direct and positive: more demand for a final product raises demand for the inputs used to make it.
If shoppers want more new cars, carmakers respond by wanting more of the inputs used to build them.
A firm's demand for labour slopes downward: when the wage rises, the quantity of labour wanted falls.

title: Effect of taxes and subsidies on price
article: Effect of taxes and subsidies on price

definition.text: How taxes and subsidies change the prices buyers pay and sellers receive, and so the quantity bought and sold.

facts.text: A tax moves the market to a new equilibrium where buyers pay more and sellers keep less.
Who legally pays the tax does not matter: a tax on sellers is largely passed on to buyers through higher prices.
Most of the burden falls on the less elastic side of the market, which is less able to change how much it buys or sells.
A specific tax shifts the supply curve up by the tax amount; an ad valorem tax, a percentage of price, also pivots it.
In one example a $0.50 tax raises the buyers' price from $3.00 to $3.30, sellers keep $2.80, and sales fall from 100 to 80.
A subsidy gives the same lower buyer price and higher seller price whether it is paid to producers or to consumers.
Tobacco taxes cut smoking: most studies find an elasticity of 0.4 to 0.5, so a 10% price rise reduces consumption by 4% to 5%.

definition.text: A measure of how much one economic variable responds to a change in another, given as the percentage change in one divided by the percentage change in the other.

facts.text: If a good's price elasticity of demand is −2, a 10% price rise cuts the quantity demanded by 20%.
The main kinds include price elasticity of demand and of supply, income elasticity of demand and cross-price elasticity of demand.
Elasticity helps explain who bears indirect taxes and how welfare is split among consumer, producer and government surplus.
Seller revenue is highest at unit elasticity: a firm should raise its price when demand is inelastic and cut it when demand is elastic.
Supply of goods made from scarce natural resources such as petrol responds poorly to demand, so rising demand drives prices up.
Time is arguably the biggest influence on supply elasticity: the longer suppliers have to respond, the more supply changes.
Alfred Marshall first described price elasticity informally in his Principles of Economics of 1890.

title: Excess supply

definition.text: A situation where sellers want to sell more of a good than buyers want to buy, because the price is above its equilibrium level; also called a market surplus or glut.

facts.text: It is the opposite of a shortage, and the two are the two kinds of disequilibrium in a competitive market.
If 1000 televisions are offered at $600 but buyers want only 300, the excess supply of 700 pushes sellers to cut the price until the market balances.
Unemployment is excess supply in the labour market, and it lowers workers' demand for goods in other markets.
Farmers face it often: a good harvest brings perishable surpluses, and governments may step in to buy them up.

notes: The page also calls this 'economic surplus', a different sense from consumer plus producer surplus.

definition.text: A market where the inputs to production, such as land, labour and capital, are bought and sold.

facts.text: Factor markets share out land, labour and capital among firms and pay income to their owners as wages, rents and the like.
Firms buy inputs in factor markets and sell the goods they make in product markets; both kinds of market work in much the same way.
A firm hires another worker when the extra revenue that worker brings in, the marginal revenue product of labour, exceeds the extra cost.
A factor in scarce supply earns a high price and an abundant one a low price, so when a factor's supply falls its equilibrium price rises.

definition.text: A market with a single dominant buyer, the buying-side mirror of a monopoly; an oligopsony has a few dominant buyers.

facts.text: A monopsonist sets the price it pays for an input instead of taking it from the market, choosing a point on the input's supply curve.
Monopsonies are more common in factor markets than in product markets, and there is growing concern about them in some kinds of labour.

title: Free market

definition.text: An economic system in which the prices of goods and services are set by the supply and demand of buyers and sellers, without government steering.

facts.text: Supporters of the free market contrast it with a regulated market, where government steps into supply and demand through taxes or rules.
In practice governments usually step in to cut harms such as greenhouse gas emissions, sometimes by using markets, as in carbon emissions trading.
Free markets are usually linked with capitalism, but they have also featured in some forms of market socialism.
To classical economists such as Adam Smith, a free market meant one free of privilege, monopolies and artificial scarcities.
A free market does not demand competition as such, but it does demand that new sellers be free to enter.
Critics say real free markets drift toward price-fixing monopolies and unequal bargaining power, which led to measures such as US antitrust law.
Coase, Friedman, von Mises and Hayek replied that markets can absorb or adjust to supposed market failures.

contested_note: Supporters say free markets create healthy competition and fair prices, while critics say they slide into monopoly and need government intervention to work.

definition.text: The principle that prices and wages should be free of non-market pressure such as government taxes, subsidies, tariffs, regulations or granted monopolies.

facts.text: Hayek argued that the point of laissez-faire is to keep the unique information that a price carries.
Karl Popper called the idea of the free market paradoxical, since it needs interventions to prevent interventions.

definition.text: The idea, popularised by Friedrich Hayek, that market economies create order through networks no one designed, which arise from many separate individual decisions.

facts.text: Hayek held that this order shares out a society's resources better than any design could.
The idea builds on Adam Smith's invisible hand from The Wealth of Nations.

definition.text: The net benefits people or economies get when they are allowed to trade more freely with each other.

facts.text: Technically, they are the rise in consumer surplus plus producer surplus from lower tariffs or freer trade.
They come from specialisation, the larger total output it allows, and selling one kind of output for other goods valued more highly.
Prices draw labour and other inputs toward activities where they have a comparative advantage, that is, a low opportunity cost.
David Ricardo first clearly stated and proved comparative advantage in 1817, the basic explanation for where gains from trade come from.
Free trade is not always best for everyone: a large economy may use taxes and subsidies to gain at other economies' expense.
Market power can let some traders block other mutually beneficial trades.

title: General equilibrium theory

definition.text: The branch of economics that studies supply, demand and prices across a whole economy of many linked markets, seeking to show that together they reach an overall equilibrium.

facts.text: It contrasts with partial equilibrium, which studies one part of the economy while holding everything else fixed.
It goes back to Léon Walras's Elements of Pure Economics of 1874 and took its modern form in the 1950s with Arrow, Debreu and McKenzie.
The first welfare theorem says market equilibria are Pareto efficient: no one can be made better off without making someone else worse off.
The first welfare theorem quietly assumes complete markets and perfect information.

The second welfare theorem says any efficient outcome can be reached by redistributing starting endowments and then leaving the market alone, suggesting efficiency and fairness can be handled separately.
From the 1970s, faster computers and input–output tables let economists solve general equilibrium models of real national and world economies numerically.
Computable general equilibrium models use real economic data to estimate how an economy might respond to changes in policy or technology.
Keynesian and Post-Keynesian economists reject the theory as misleading, arguing that real economies are not in equilibrium.

contested_note: General equilibrium theory is a central dispute between neoclassical economists and other schools, some of which call it misleading and useless.

title: Imperfect competition

definition.text: Any market that falls short of at least one of the conditions of a perfectly competitive market.

facts.text: Imperfect competition makes markets inefficient and so leads to market failure.
A market is imperfect if sellers can set their own prices, there is only one seller, entry is blocked, buyers and sellers know different things, or products differ.
The more a firm can lift price above marginal cost, the greater the inefficiency; at the extreme, a monopoly overcharges and underproduces.
The broad imperfect market structures include monopolistic competition, where many firms sell slightly different products, and oligopoly, where a few firms each sway the others.
A firm in an imperfect market faces a downward-sloping demand curve, unlike the flat demand curve facing a perfectly competitive firm.
Some theorists hold that no real market has ever met the conditions of perfect competition.

contested_note: Economists dispute whether economic policy should assume perfect or imperfect competition.

definition.text: A measure of how concentrated a market is, found by adding up the squares of every firm's market share.

facts.text: It gives big firms more weight than a simple concentration ratio does.
It runs from 1/N to 1, where N is the number of firms; the more concentrated the market, the higher the value.

definition.text: How strongly the quantity of a good people buy responds to a change in their income.

facts.text: It is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in income: if a 10% rise in income lifts demand by 20%, it is 2.0.
Normal goods have positive income elasticity and inferior goods negative; below 1 marks a necessity and above 1 a luxury.
Food as a whole has an income elasticity between zero and one, so spending on food grows more slowly than income, an observation called Engel's law.
Estimates for gasoline in developed economies range from 0.66 to 1.26.
Income elasticities for food and energy tend to fall as incomes rise: for cereals, from 0.62 in Tanzania to 0.05 in the United States.
As economies get richer, spending shifts toward services, which need fewer commodities to produce.
Most measures of environmental damage rise with income, though with an income elasticity below one.

title: Inverse demand function

definition.text: A formula that gives price as a function of the quantity demanded, so it is also called a price function.

facts.text: Its value is the highest price that could be charged while still selling that quantity; it equals the average revenue function.
It is found by solving the demand function for price: if Q = 240 − 2P, then P = 120 − Q/2.
For a straight-line demand P = a − bQ, marginal revenue is MR = a − 2bQ: the same starting height and twice the slope.
It is used to find the profit-maximising output, where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, and then the price to charge.

notes: Sentence afe171025897 renders the inverse as 'P=120−12Q', a lost fraction (1/2 Q); the fact paraphrases it as Q/2, which is what 240 − 2P solved for P gives and what the TR line e9be0558cc94 implies. Verify.

title: Invisible hand

definition.text: Adam Smith's metaphor for the way free markets can lead self-interested people to serve the public good without meaning to.

facts.text: Smith used the phrase only once each in The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759) and The Wealth of Nations, and spoke of 'an' invisible hand, never 'the'.
In The Wealth of Nations it appears in a chapter about where merchants invest their capital, not about free trade.
Paul Samuelson's 1948 textbook popularised the phrase and gave it a new meaning: that free markets regulate themselves and reach outcomes government cannot improve.
The idea that market exchange channels self-interest toward social good is a central justification for laissez-faire thinking behind neoclassical economics.
Joseph Stiglitz argues the hand often seems invisible because it is not there: with externalities, markets on their own produce too much pollution.
Environmental economics deals largely with market failures, where the invisible hand is unreliable.

contested_note: Economists such as Stiglitz and Piketty argue that markets often fail to turn self-interest into social good, and scholars disagree about what Smith himself meant.

definition.text: The basic rule that, all else being equal, people buy less of a good when its price rises and more when it falls.

facts.text: It says only which way quantity moves when price changes, not by how much.
It is drawn as the demand curve, with quantity on the horizontal axis and price on the vertical, which slopes downward.
A price change moves buyers along the demand curve; changes in the number of buyers, income, tastes, prices of related goods or expectations shift the whole curve.
Charles Davenant first stated it in 1699, and Alfred Marshall drew it as a graph and joined it with supply in his Principles of Economics (1890).
Together with the law of supply, it fixes the equilibrium price and quantity.
Exceptions include Giffen goods, Veblen goods, necessities and cases where buyers expect prices to keep changing.

definition.text: A luxury good whose demand rises as its price rises, because a high price signals status.

facts.text: Examples include diamonds, gold, precious stones, famous paintings and antiques.
Thorstein Veblen described such buying as paying for status and social position rather than extra usefulness.

title: Law of supply

definition.text: The basic rule that, all else being equal, a higher price leads sellers to offer more of a good.

facts.text: Producers offer more at higher prices because producing more is a way to make more profit; this is why the supply curve slopes upward.
A job paying £20 an hour draws more interest than one paying £15 an hour.
Things other than price shift the supply curve: production costs, the number of suppliers, subsidies, taxes and, in farming, the weather.
If buyers want more than sellers offer, the price rises, cutting demand and raising supply until the two match.
Some heterodox economists, such as Steve Keen, argue the supply curve for mass-produced goods often slopes downward.

contested_note: Some heterodox economists dispute the law of supply for mass-produced goods, whose unit prices may fall as output grows.

definition.text: The extra revenue a firm earns by selling one more unit of its product.

facts.text: In a perfectly competitive market a firm gets the same price for every unit, so its marginal revenue equals the price.
A monopoly must cut its price on all units to sell one more, so its marginal revenue is always below the price.
Example: selling 20 books at $50 brings $1000, and 21 books at $49 brings $1029, so the 21st book adds $29.
A firm maximises profit where marginal revenue equals marginal cost; it is making money on extra units while marginal revenue is higher.
When demand is inelastic, selling more forces a price cut on every unit and marginal revenue turns negative.
Under perfect competition the marginal revenue curve is a flat line at the market price; for a monopoly it slopes down and lies below the demand curve.

definition.text: A measure of market power: the gap between price and marginal cost as a share of price, named after economist Abba Lerner.

facts.text: At the profit-maximising point, (P − MC)/P equals minus one over the elasticity of demand, so less elastic demand means a higher markup.
It runs from zero in a perfectly competitive market to 1; the closer to 1, the bigger the gap between price and marginal cost.

title: Market clearing

definition.text: The process by which a market's price settles where the amount supplied equals the amount demanded, leaving neither a surplus nor a shortage.

facts.text: The market-clearing price, also called the equilibrium price, is the one at which quantity supplied equals quantity demanded.
A price above it builds up unsold stock; a price below it leaves buyers short, sometimes unable to find the product at any price.
After an earthquake destroys homes, a housing shortage pushes prices up, builders build more, and supply rises until it meets the new demand.
Shops discount leftover Christmas decorations after Christmas until shoppers buy the excess supply.
From about 1785 to 1935 most economists took market clearing for granted, until the Great Depression's long mass unemployment led Keynes and others to doubt it.
Most economists now see continuous market clearing as unrealistic but useful for long-run analysis.

contested_note: Since the Great Depression economists have disagreed over whether prices adjust quickly enough for markets to clear, with some blaming sticky prices and others blaming unions or government policy.

definition.text: An economic system in which decisions about investment, production and distribution are guided by prices set through supply and demand.

facts.text: Market economies range from barely regulated free-market systems to interventionist ones where governments correct market failures and promote welfare.
They need clearly defined, enforceable property rights, though these need not be private: co-operatives and state firms can also trade in markets.
A price system signals people to adjust what they produce and invest; strong demand with limited supply pushes prices up and invites more production.
Governments can set price ceilings or floors, such as minimum wages, or use Pigovian taxes to deal with externalities.
Joseph Stiglitz argues markets suffer from imperfect information and need government action to fix widespread market failures.
A sustainable market economy tries to balance growth with environmental protection, using tax incentives, carbon trading and environmental rules.

definition.text: The way buyers and sellers exchanging money for goods, at prices that reflect value and scarcity, tends to share out goods and services well.

facts.text: Prices tell producers what people want, and the less accurate that information, the worse the coordination and the fewer wants are met.
The market mechanism often cannot provide public goods well, because of problems such as the tragedy of the commons; highways needed government planning.
Free market economies leave resources to the private sector, planned economies to the public sector, and mixed economies to both.

definition.text: A firm's ability to raise the price of what it sells above its marginal cost, by controlling supply or demand, without losing all its customers.

facts.text: Firms with no market power, as in perfect competition, are price takers; firms with it are price makers.
How much power firms have depends on market structure: perfect competition and monopoly are the extremes, with monopolistic competition and oligopoly in between.
Power lasts only behind barriers to entry, such as control of scarce resources, economies of scale, better technology or government rules; OPEC's power comes from controlling oil.
It is measured by markups, or more often by concentration ratios and the Herfindahl-Hirschman index, which need only revenue data.
The less elastic the demand a firm faces, the more it can raise price above marginal cost.
Competition law, such as the US Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890, uses measures of market power to judge whether a firm has abused it.
Jean Tirole won the 2014 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for analysing market power and regulation.

definition.text: The combined market share of the largest few firms in a market, such as the top four.

facts.text: The four-firm ratio is 100 per cent for a monopoly and zero for perfect competition.
Studies suggest a ratio between 40 and 70 percent points to an oligopoly.
Concentration measures are the most common gauge of market power because they need only revenue data, though they ignore costs and profits.

definition.text: An analysis of equilibrium in a single market that holds everything else constant except the one change being studied.

facts.text: Alfred Marshall's supply and demand model is the classic partial equilibrium model.
It treats the prices of substitutes and complements and buyers' incomes as given, which makes it much simpler than general equilibrium.
A tariff on French wine raises its price; partial equilibrium ignores the knock-on rise in demand for domestic wine that feeds back and pushes the price higher still.
Such feedback usually changes the size of a price change but not its direction.

title: Price ceiling

definition.text: A limit, set by government or another body, on the highest price that may be charged for a product or service.

facts.text: Governments set price ceilings to protect consumers from goods becoming too expensive.
Economists generally agree that consumer price controls fail at their aims, and many advise against them.
A ceiling set below the market equilibrium price leads to a shortage of supply.
Ceilings can even raise prices by giving competing firms a shared target to collude on; US states with an 18 percent interest cap saw rates just below it.
Ceilings on Helsinki's Hitas apartments cause queuing and mean flats do not go to those who value them most.
Venezuela's food price ceilings from 2003 caused shortages and hoarding.
Some economists, such as Isabella Weber, argue for price caps to fight sellers' inflation, and Paul Krugman became open to them.

contested_note: Most economists say price ceilings backfire, but some, such as Isabella Weber and later Paul Krugman, support price caps against inflation.

definition.text: A price ceiling on housing rents, such as the US rent controls of the 1940s brought in under Franklin D. Roosevelt's Office of Price Administration.

facts.text: As economic models predicted, the US controls cut the supply of rental homes available to returning veterans.
Homeownership and homes for sale rose at the same time, likely because landlords turned rentals into homes for sale.

title: Price controls

definition.text: Government-enforced limits on the prices that may be charged for goods and services in a market.

facts.text: There are two main kinds: a price ceiling sets the most that may be charged and a price floor the least; rent control and the minimum wage are well-known examples.
They aim to keep goods affordable during shortages, slow inflation, or guarantee a minimum income to some providers.
Price controls are ancient: the Code of Hammurabi set wages for shipbuilders, and Diocletian tried to cap the price of every commodity in the late 3rd century AD, with little success.
Keeping prices artificially low raises demand beyond what supply can meet, causing shortages, and shortages feed black markets with higher prices.
During the 1973–74 Arab oil embargo, a US price cap below the market level led to long queues and gas stations running dry.
Western economists generally hold that consumer price controls fail, though since the 1990s minimum wages have won strong support among some economists.
Price controls are one of the indirect ways governments subsidise energy.

contested_note: Most Western economists say consumer price controls do not work, while some support minimum wages and other price caps.

definition.text: A pricing strategy in which the same seller charges different buyers different prices for the same or nearly the same good, according to which group they seem to belong to.

facts.text: It works by exploiting differences in buyers' willingness to pay and in how sensitive they are to price.
The seller needs market power; otherwise buyers would switch sellers or resell cheap units to those charged more.
In first-degree, or perfect, price discrimination each buyer pays their maximum, so the seller captures all consumer surplus.
Second-degree discrimination varies price with the quantity bought; third-degree charges different groups different prices, as with student and senior discounts.
The aim is to raise profit by shifting consumer surplus to the seller.
Drug-makers charge more in wealthier countries; antiretroviral drugs cost far less in Africa, where sales would otherwise be very limited.
The first-, second- and third-degree categories are attributed to Pigou.

definition.text: How strongly the quantity sellers offer responds to a change in price: the percentage change in quantity supplied for a 1% change in price.

facts.text: Supply is inelastic below 1, elastic above 1, unit-elastic at exactly 1, and fixed at zero, when quantity does not respond at all.
Unlike demand elasticities, supply elasticities are usually positive, because a higher price encourages more production.
Some goods barely respond to price: a country's gold output may be capped by availability, and no price will produce more Van Gogh paintings.
Supply is usually more elastic in the long run, when all inputs can be expanded, than in the short run.
Spare capacity makes supply more elastic; once capacity is full, more output needs new investment, so supply becomes less elastic.
The more elastic housing supply is, the smaller the rent rise needed to clear a shortage after demand grows.
Land is the classic example of a factor whose supply is inelastic.

definition.text: A limit, set by government or another body, on the lowest price that may be charged for a product or service.

facts.text: A floor only bites if it is set above the equilibrium price; set below it, it has no practical effect.
Common examples are minimum wage laws, supply management in Canadian farming, US airfares before 1978 and minimum prices for alcohol.
A binding floor makes buyers buy less while sellers want to sell more, leaving a lasting surplus.
It shifts some consumer surplus to producers and creates a deadweight loss.
EU support buying to hold farm prices at an intervention price has sometimes left 'butter mountains' of surplus in warehouses.
Hybrid cap-and-trade schemes add floor and ceiling prices to steady the carbon price.
Before deregulation in 1978, US airfare floors kept flying so costly that in 1965 more than 80% of Americans had never flown on a jet.

title: Minimum wage

definition.text: A price floor for labour: the lowest hourly rate an employer is allowed by law to pay.

facts.text: Set above the market wage for low-skilled work, it leads employers to hire fewer workers, for example by switching to self-service or machines.
The higher wage also draws more people into the labour market, producing a surplus of labour.
Since the credibility revolution of the 1990s, minimum wages have often won strong support among economists.

contested_note: Standard theory predicts a minimum wage above the market wage cuts jobs, yet since the 1990s many economists have strongly supported minimum wages.

definition.text: The way prices decide how resources are shared out and steer how much of each good is supplied and demanded.

facts.text: Prices match buyers and sellers in three ways: as an incentive, as a signal and as a way of rationing resources.
At competitive equilibrium, the value society puts on a good equals the value of the resources used to make it, which is allocative efficiency.
The 1970s oil crisis drove oil prices up, prompting several countries to start producing their own oil.
Dearer fuel does not quickly cut demand, but over time it pushes firms to offer alternatives such as biodiesel and electric cars.
An auction is a price mechanism in which bidders compete and the highest bid wins.
Greenhouse gas cap-and-trade applies the idea to emissions, as the US did earlier with sulfur dioxide, cutting overall smog.
Ludwig von Mises argued that planned economies reject the price mechanism and so cannot allocate resources rationally.

definition.text: The information a price carries to buyers and sellers, telling them to supply or demand more or less of something.

facts.text: When a product runs short and its price rises, people pay more attention to it and produce more of it.
Prices coordinate what is produced, how it is produced and what resources are used.
Friedrich Hayek argued that prices let people share knowledge spread among many others and coordinate their separate actions.
Monopolies, cartels and monopsonies can set prices that do not reflect production costs, weakening the signal.
Credit bubbles and speculation can distort price signals, leading to waste and financial crises.
Fuel taxes send price signals that make consumers aware of hidden costs such as greenhouse gases and other pollution.
Electricity users react little to price in the short run because they do not face the actual cost of production at each moment.

definition.text: What a business has left from its revenue after paying the total costs of its inputs, counting both explicit and implicit costs.

facts.text: Accounting profit subtracts only the explicit costs on a firm's books; economic profit also subtracts implicit costs, so it is smaller.
Normal profit is when revenue just equals total costs, so economic profit is zero: the least a firm needs to stay in a competitive industry.
In a perfectly competitive market, economic profit draws in new firms until prices fall and the profit disappears in the long run.
Economic profit lasts in uncompetitive markets such as monopolies and oligopolies, protected by barriers to entry like patents, land rights and zoning laws.
Economists usually assume firms try to maximise profit, which happens where marginal revenue equals marginal cost.
A firm's social profit is its accounting profit plus or minus the externalities, such as pollution, and consumer surplus its activity creates.
Competition laws aim to stop powerful firms from building artificial barriers to entry to protect their profits.

definition.text: A situation in which people want to buy more of a product than is available at the going price; also called excess demand.

facts.text: It is the opposite of an excess supply, or surplus.
In a simple market, excess demand pushes the price up until demand matches supply; a shortage persists only when something stops the price rising.
Then something other than price, such as first come first served or a lottery, decides who gets the good.
Causes include price ceilings, bans on selling a product and suppliers choosing not to raise prices.
Shortages bring black markets, queues and rationing, more demand for substitutes, and wasted time that lowers overall wealth.
In the 1980s Soviet Union, prices fixed artificially low left people queuing for cars, apartments and clothing.
Economists and historians note that lasting shortages and famines have mostly been caused by war, price controls and repressive regimes rather than overpopulation.

definition.text: The amount of something that producers, workers or other sellers are willing and able to offer for sale.

facts.text: Supply is usually drawn as a supply curve, with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis, for one seller or the whole market.
Supply depends on the good's own price, the prices of related goods, production costs, technology and sellers' expectations.
A change in the good's own price moves sellers along the curve; a change in anything else shifts the whole curve, as when a costlier ingredient shifts it left.
A firm's short-run supply curve is its marginal cost curve above the point where it would shut down.
The market supply curve adds up the quantities all firms would supply at each price.
A supply curve exists only under perfect competition; a monopoly has none, because it picks price and quantity together.
Where there are no externalities, the supply curve shows the social cost of each extra unit.

definition.text: The lowest cost of producing a given amount of output, made up of variable costs plus fixed costs.

facts.text: Variable costs, such as labour and raw materials, change with output; fixed costs, such as buildings and machinery, do not in the short term.
In economics it includes the opportunity cost of every input, the benefit of its next-best use.
The extra total cost of one more unit is the marginal cost.
Long-run total cost is generally lower than short-run, because the amount of capital can be chosen to suit the output.

definition.text: The state an industry reaches when firms can enter or leave it almost freely, so that competition pushes each firm's economic profit to zero.

facts.text: If firms earn positive economic profit, newcomers join until it is gone; if they make losses, firms leave until profit rises back to zero.
The zero-profit situation is called the industry's long run and is close to perfect competition.
In gold rushes few prospectors got rich, but many people built successful businesses selling shovels.
In neoclassical models, a market economy of profit-seeking firms is compatible with zero growth because of this condition.

contested_note: Economists have offered conflicting definitions of a barrier to entry since the 1950s with no consensus.
title: Barriers to entry

definition.text: A fixed cost a new entrant must bear to enter a market that incumbents do not bear or have not had to bear.

facts.text: By protecting incumbents and restricting competition, barriers to entry can distort prices, which is why they matter most in antitrust policy.
Barriers to entry often cause or help sustain monopolies and oligopolies, or give firms market power.
Governments can also erect barriers to entry, for instance to meet consumer protection laws.
Definitions conflict: Bain (1956), Stigler (1968), Fisher (1979), Baumol and Willig (1981) and others each gave one, and no consensus exists on which to use.
A primary barrier is a cost that is a barrier on its own; an ancillary barrier only reinforces other barriers that are present.

A structural barrier comes from inherent industry conditions such as upfront capital, economies of scale and network effects; a strategic barrier is created or raised by existing firms, for example by exclusive contracts.
Perfect competition has zero barriers to entry; monopolistic competition allows medium barriers; oligopoly typically has high ones.
Porter classes markets by entry and exit barriers; the higher both are, the more prone a market is to natural monopoly, and the lower, the nearer to perfect competition.

definition.text: A clandestine market or set of transactions with some aspect of illegality within a legal jurisdiction.

facts.text: Transactions in goods whose production or distribution the law prohibits or restricts are black-market trade because the exchange itself is illegal.
Black-market goods may be cheaper than legal ones because suppliers avoid production costs and taxes.
Illegal logging is, according to Interpol, an industry worth almost as much as drug production in some countries.
In many developing countries wild animals are captured and sold as pets, or hunted for meat, hides and organs used in traditional medicine.

definition.text: An organization that maintains the infrastructure for a public service, often also providing the service itself.

facts.text: Utilities supply goods considered essential, such as water, gas, electricity, telephone and waste disposal, and are subject to public control or regulation.
Electricity transmission lines and natural gas pipelines have natural monopoly traits: where infrastructure exists, competing brings little benefit.
Utilities are capital-intensive, with large economies of scale and high fixed costs for plants, lines and treatment facilities.
Modern utilities may draw partly or wholly on clean and renewable energy, mostly wind turbines and solar panels.

In OECD countries, wholesale electricity generation has become far more decentralised with solar and wind power, while distribution and transmission networks often stay centralised and need heavy government involvement.

In the US, FERC Order No. 888 (1996) required electric utilities to open their transmission systems and unbundle transmission from other operations, restructuring the regulated monopoly toward competition among bulk sellers.
US public utilities commissions regulate electric, gas, telecom, water and rail companies, approving or denying rate increases on behalf of ratepayers.

definition.text: Ways regulators set the prices a utility may charge, such as average-cost pricing, rate-of-return limits and price caps.

facts.text: Average-cost pricing sets the price equal to average production cost at the break-even point, serving most of the market, but regulated firms then lack incentive to minimise costs.

Rate-of-return regulation lets firms set any price so long as the return on invested capital stays under a cap; it is flexible but can cause overcapitalization, since investing more capital raises the allowed profit.
Price cap regulation directly sets a maximum price, which can result in a loss of service area.
